research:continuum.area: Continuum and particle methods for simulating matter in real time (MPM family, SPH, PBF/PBD, real-time FEM, fracture, phase change, unified frameworks) and their fit to a base iPhone 15 (A16)
research:continuum.summary:
Verification caveat first: direct page fetch was blocked in this session (arxiv.org and www.math.ucla.edu are outside the allowed network domains and would have to be allowed in the session's network settings; the GitHub tool is restricted to the user's repo). Every item marked verified=true was confirmed only through WebSearch extracts quoting the cited source, not a full-page read; derived arithmetic and memory items are marked verified=false. Several wanted numbers could not be retrieved (Fei 2021 single-GPU per-substep timings, Flex Table 1, XPBI timings, CD-MPM timings).

Conclusion: no single discretization is a credible sole substrate for matter at real stiffness on a phone-class GPU. The binding constraint is wave speed, not particle count: an explicit solver at 1 cm resolution would need roughly 2,500 (water) to 9,800 (steel) substeps per 60 Hz frame, against the 2-4 that real-time demos budget. All real-time systems cope by one of three routes: softening moduli by orders of magnitude, implicit or position-based solves whose effective stiffness depends on iteration budget, or idealizing stiff matter as rigid.

The most credible design is two-tier, unified by one SI material and constitutive library rather than one solver:
- Flowing and breaking matter (liquids, granular, snow, mud, soft and plastic solids, melting): MLS-MPM/APIC, ideally in a time-step-robust form (PB-MPM-style or implicit), because it needs no neighbor search, handles topology change and self-collision for free, and takes the widest range of constitutive models.
- Stiff structural matter and mechanisms: rigid bodies plus an implicit constraint/FEM solver (AVBD/VBD/XPBD family), coupled to MPM through explicit frictional contact.
State-of-the-art "unified" engines in 2026 (Newton 1.x, Genesis) are themselves multi-solver, which supports this.

Phone-scale sizing is an estimate, not a measurement: no iPhone MPM benchmark exists in the literature found. Anchors are a WebGPU MLS-MPM demo at about 100k particles on a laptop integrated GPU at 2 steps per frame, and a vendor statement of "tens of thousands of particles on mobile". A planning figure of about 50-100k MPM particles at 60 Hz implies dx of 2-5 cm, an active window of 64^3 to 128^3 cells (1.3-2.6 m cube at 2 cm; 3.2-6.4 m at 5 cm), and only about 0.1 m^3 of actual matter at 2 cm (about 1.5 m^3 at 5 cm) at 8 particles per cell. That is a tabletop-to-room-corner sandbox; everything else must be rigid, sleeping or analytic.

findings.claim: Derived CFL bound (dt <= dx/c): with longitudinal sound speed about 5,900 m/s in steel and 1,482 m/s in water, a 1 cm grid needs dt <= 1.7 microseconds (steel) or 6.7 microseconds (water), i.e. at least ~9,800 or ~2,500 explicit substeps per 60 Hz frame before any safety factor. Real-time demos budget 2-4 substeps.
findings.source: Derived; sound speeds from https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/sound/souspe2.html and https://www.engineeringtoolbox.com/sound-speed-solids-d_713.html (search extracts)

findings.claim: Fei, Huang, Gao 2021 (the reference real-time GPU MPM paper) reports a 1.33M-particle snow scene at 68.5 fps and a 143K-particle fountain at 55.9 fps on four Tesla V100 GPUs with NVLink, not one GPU, plus 1.7-8.6x single-GPU speedup over prior art. The smaller fluid scene being slower than the larger snow scene suggests substep count, not particle count, dominates cost (my inference).

A WebGPU MLS-MPM fluid demo (matsuoka-601 WebGPU-Ocean, Jan-Feb 2025) runs about 100k particles in real time on a Ryzen 7 5825U integrated GPU, about 300k on mid-range GPUs and 500k on an RTX 3060 Laptop, at 2 simulation steps per frame with atomicAdd-based P2G. The same author's SPH version reached only about 30k particles on the iGPU because neighbor search was the bottleneck.

No published MPM benchmark on an iPhone or A16 was found. The closest mobile data point is Zibra (MLS-MPM/APIC-based, supports iOS Metal arm64) stating "tens of thousands of particles on mobile devices" versus hundreds of thousands on laptops; the A16 5-core GPU scores about 2,900-3,360 in 3DMark Wild Life Extreme.

Current "unified" engines are multi-solver, not single-substrate. Newton (1.0 GA at GTC March 2026, v1.5.0 in Aug 2026, Linux Foundation since 2025-09-29, Apache-2.0, requires warp-lang>=1.16) ships XPBD, VBD, semi-implicit, implicit MPM and MuJoCo Warp solvers, with VBD and MPM coupled to MuJoCo Warp explicitly; Genesis lists separate Rigid, MPM, SPH, FEM, PBD and Stable Fluid solvers.

PB-MPM (Lewin, EA SEED, SIGGRAPH 2024 Talk) is a semi-implicit compliant-constraint MPM described as "stable at any time-step", with one Jacobi-style iteration costing about one explicit MPM step, covering liquids, elastic solids, sand and visco-plastics. The public code is 2D WebGPU (BSD-3; EA's 3D version is in-house CPU), and a later paper criticizes it for PBD-style non-physical parameters and iteration-dependent stiffness.

MLS-MPM (Hu et al. 2018) gives about a 2x speedup over traditional MPM with almost identical visual results and derives APIC/PolyPIC from one discretization. Its CPIC extension adds cutting, thin boundaries and two-way rigid-body coupling.

Particle-grid transfer choice sets the dissipation artifact: PIC dissipates angular momentum severely, FLIP keeps energy but is noisy, and APIC conserves linear and angular momentum with FLIP-like dissipation and no noise. PolyPIC generalizes APIC to polynomial modes for better energy and vorticity conservation.

Explicit MPM stability is not guaranteed by the CFL condition alone. Sun et al. 2020 note graphics time steps are usually chosen by trial and error and that a splashing-fluid case needed an extra single-particle restriction; Bai and Schroeder 2022 find boundaries less stable than interiors and pathological growth with APIC/CPIC at arbitrarily small time steps.

Documented non-physical MPM artifacts: cell-crossing instability from discontinuous linear shape-function gradients (mitigated by GIMP, CPDI or B-spline kernels), numerical fracture when particles separate beyond kernel support (CPDI does not fully remove it), and volumetric locking near incompressibility (needs an F-bar-type fix; higher-order bases alone do not cure it).

MPM's built-in contact is sticky: single-velocity-field MPM prevents interpenetration for free but only models stick contact with no tangential slip, and suffers premature contact detection at grid-cell distance. Frictional sliding needs multi-field MPM or an explicit coupling scheme.

Offline-scale GPU MPM references: Gao 2018 ran 4.2M particles on a 256^3 grid with implicit dynamics and heat at 10.5 s per 48 Hz frame on a Quadro P6000; Wang 2020 ran about 100M particles on 1024^3 in under 4 min/frame on 4 GPUs (110-120x per-step over SIMD CPU). QuanTaichi fit 235M particles on one GPU through quantization.

Recent MPM work: CK-MPM (TOG 2025) uses a C2 compact kernel on a dual grid for about 2x faster G2P2G than quadratic B-splines but tends to promote fracture; MPM Lite (arXiv Feb 2026) uses linear kernels for 1.69x explicit and up to 15.9x implicit speedup at 24 particles per cell. A May 2026 sparse framework uses GPU hashing for 1-2 orders of magnitude savings in strongly sparse scenes, and "Substepping the MPM" (Aug 2025) wraps explicit substeps into a pseudo-implicit macro step.

Implicit MPM is the published answer to stiffness: HOT (Wang 2020) states explicit MPM needs time steps far below CFL for stiff materials such as metal and is up to 10x faster than prior implicit MPM codes. Newton's SolverImplicitMPM (after Daviet and Bertails-Descoubes 2016, Drucker-Prager rheology) is documented as unconditionally stable in dt and best for very stiff or fully inelastic materials, but less versatile than explicit MPM, with a default of 250 rheology iterations.

Rigid-MPM coupling precedent for mechanisms acting on matter: the Drake convex formulation (Yu et al. 2025) integrates MPM explicitly at small steps on GPU and rigid bodies at larger steps via asynchronous time-splitting, reporting up to 500x speedup over the earlier convex formulation. It ships in open-source Drake.

Vertex Block Descent (SIGGRAPH 2024) is an unconditionally stable block-coordinate descent on implicit Euler; its largest scene (48M vertices, 151M tetrahedra) takes 3.6 s per step, i.e. offline. The authors report poor convergence at a 1:10000 stiffness ratio and call it not ideal for high-resolution stiff systems.

Augmented VBD (Giles, Diaz, Yuksel, SIGGRAPH 2025) adds augmented-Lagrangian hard constraints and simulates 110,000 rigid blocks in 3.5 ms (9.8 ms with collision detection) and 510,000 in 10.3 ms (17.6 ms) per frame on an RTX 4090 with 4 iterations. This is the strongest published real-time result for stiff bodies and joints.

XPBD replaces PBD's iteration- and time-step-dependent stiffness with a compliance (inverse stiffness in physical units), but it only matches the physical answer at convergence. "Small Steps" (Macklin 2019) shows n substeps of 1 iteration beat 1 step of n iterations (30x1 at 13.5 ms was visibly stiffer than 1x30 at 12.4 ms).
findings.source: https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/XPBD.pdf ; https://diglib.eg.org/handle/10.1145/3309486-3340247 (search extracts; timing example from an unofficial copy)

findings.claim: Constitutive coverage differs by solver family: stable Neo-Hookean (Smith 2018) handles Poisson ratio near 0.5, inversion and rest stability, and Macklin and Mueller 2021 reproduce it in XPBD as deviatoric plus hydrostatic constraints. Projective Dynamics does not support Neo-Hookean or Mooney-Rivlin (Liu 2017), and XPBD is limited to energies quadratic in a constraint.

Unified Particle Physics / Flex (Macklin 2014, SIGGRAPH 2025 Test-of-Time award) ran real time on a GTX 680 at 16 ms frames, with a 300k-particle Rayleigh-Taylor scene at about 150 ms per frame. Its rigid bodies use shape matching, whose cost grows with particle count, propagates impulses slowly and handles joints poorly; Position Based Fluids explicitly trades incompressibility for speed.

Incompressible SPH is accurate but offline at scale: DFSPH holds volume compression below 0.01% with over 20x speedup against then-current SPH (5M fluid plus 40M boundary particles at 5 s per step), and IISPH ran 30M particles at 44 s per step with dt = 4 ms and under 0.1% compression on a 16-core PC. Weakly compressible SPH instead uses a Tait equation of state with an artificial sound speed to trade a Poisson solve for small user-defined density fluctuations.

First-principles fracture is not demonstrated in real time: CD-MPM (Wolper 2019) offers a phase-field model needing a coupled momentum/damage solve and a Non-Associated Cam-Clay plasticity model, shown at 7.79M particles. Peridynamics in graphics (Levine 2014, Chen 2018) is a trivially parallel explicit spring-mass-like scheme with a von-Neumann-bounded time step; no mobile or real-time results were found for either.

Phase change from first principles exists for MPM: Augmented MPM (Stomakhin 2014) solves the heat equation rho*c*DT/Dt = div(kappa*grad T) implicitly on the grid, tracks latent heat L in a per-particle buffer, varies Young's modulus and Poisson ratio with temperature and phase, and adds a MAC-grid Chorin projection for incompressibility. Gao 2018's 4.2M-particle melting demo used this class of solver at 10.5 s per frame.

Plasticity models consume few measurable parameters: the Stomakhin 2013 snow model uses critical compression 2.5e-2, critical stretch 7.5e-3 and hardening coefficient 10; Drucker-Prager sand (Klar 2016, Hencky-strain elasticity) takes the friction angle phi through alpha = sqrt(2/3)*2*sin(phi)/(3 - sin(phi)).

From memory: the snow paper's elastic parameters are E0 = 1.4e5 Pa, density 400 kg/m^3 and Poisson ratio 0.2. The full parameter set a first-principles material library needs is density, Young's modulus and Poisson ratio (Lame parameters), von Mises yield stress and hardening, friction angle and cohesion, bulk modulus and Tait exponent (gamma = 7 for water), dynamic viscosity (Herschel-Bulkley yield stress, consistency and flow index for non-Newtonian fluids), fracture energy or critical stretch, and conductivity, specific heat and latent heat.

Typical real-time MPM demos use non-SI softened moduli tuned to sit at the CFL limit: Taichi's mpm128 example uses 9,000 particles on a 128^2 grid in a unit domain with E = 5e3, nu = 0.2 and dt = 1e-4 (the 88-line variant uses E = 400, dt = 2e-4, 8,192 particles).

Derived stiffness ceiling at a phone budget: with dx = 2 cm and 4 explicit substeps per 60 Hz frame, wave speed must stay below about 4.8 m/s, i.e. a P-wave modulus of about 23 kPa at 1000 kg/m^3, roughly 10^5 times softer than water's 2.2 GPa bulk modulus. The published snow parameters would need at least ~16 substeps per frame at that resolution.
findings.source: Derived from the CFL condition and the parameters above; water bulk modulus consistent with https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/sound/souspe2.html

findings.claim: Genesis's headline speed (43M FPS for a Franka arm on an RTX 4090) was disputed: an independent test with realistic settings measured about 0.29M FPS (150x lower) and found it 3-10x slower than ManiSkill on manipulation. Its README lists CPU, Nvidia/AMD GPU and Apple Metal backends.

Taichi AOT is a documented route for compiled simulation kernels on mobile (official Android/Vulkan walkthrough with an implicit FEM demo, a Metal backend, OPPO wallpapers shipped via ti.aot.Module), but no phone MPM benchmark was found.

XPBI (Yu et al. 2024) brings updated-Lagrangian elastoplasticity (sand, snow, plasticine) into XPBD alongside cloth and water, but its authors state the grid-colored Gauss-Seidel solver performs poorly on small cases on GPUs and that a tailored real-time solver is future work.

implications: Do not promise one solver for all matter. Plan a two-tier substrate unified by one SI material database and constitutive library: an MLS-MPM/APIC tier for matter that flows, piles, tears or melts, and a rigid plus implicit-constraint tier (AVBD/VBD/XPBD family) for stiff structural matter and mechanisms, which is where the "robot on top of reality" parts live.

State the wave-speed compromise explicitly as the one sanctioned departure from real parameters. Keep density, gravity, friction angle, yield and strength, viscosity and thermal properties real; cap elastic wave speed (the standard rule from memory is sound speed about 10x the maximum flow speed for about 1% density error); treat truly stiff solids as rigid or as implicit compliance.

Softening a modulus while keeping a real yield stress changes the yield strain, so the material library needs a defined scaling rule that preserves the visible dimensionless groups (Froude number, friction angle, strength over rho*g*L) and relaxes the invisible ones (Mach number).

Plan around roughly 50-100k MPM particles with 2-4 substeps or a handful of implicit iterations per 60 Hz frame, and treat this as an unmeasured estimate. Memory is not the constraint (about 100 bytes per particle plus a 128^3 grid is tens of MB); GPU throughput and thermal throttling are.

Design the world as a small materialized MPM window (64^3 dense to 128^3 sparse cells at dx 2-5 cm) inside a larger rigid, sleeping or analytic world, with matter promoted into MPM near interactions and demoted afterwards. At 8 particles per cell, 100k particles is only about 0.1 m^3 of matter at 2 cm.

Prefer a time-step-robust MPM formulation (PB-MPM-style constraints, implicit MPM, or a pressure projection for liquids) over pure explicit integration, since explicit weakly compressible water at phone budgets will be visibly compressible. The cost is iteration-dependent effective stiffness, which must be measured and reported, not hidden.

Use APIC/MLS-MPM transfers and quadratic B-splines as the baseline to avoid PIC dissipation and cell-crossing, add an F-bar-type fix for near-incompressible materials, and evaluate compact or linear kernels (CK-MPM, MPM Lite) for mobile cost with the known risk of extra numerical fracture.

Mechanism-on-matter interaction needs an explicit two-way rigid-MPM coupling with Coulomb friction (CPIC or Drake-style asynchronous coupling), because native MPM contact is sticky and acts at grid-cell distance.

Fracture on the phone should come from plasticity with softening or critical-stretch damage in the MPM tier and energy-criterion breakage in the stiff tier. Phase-field and peridynamic fracture have no real-time evidence, and MPM fracture is resolution-dependent unless regularized.

Newton/Warp, Genesis and Flex are reference implementations and validation oracles for the Linux dev box, not shippable phone runtimes; the phone solver will have to be hand-written GPU compute. The only quantitative small-GPU data found comes from WebGPU implementations (WebGPU-Ocean, PB-MPM), which also suits a Linux-only dev environment.

Build a first-principles validation suite early: mass, momentum and angular momentum conservation, energy drift, hydrostatic pressure, dam break, granular column collapse versus friction angle, beam deflection versus Euler-Bernoulli, Stokes terminal velocity. Numerical dissipation at cm resolution means real water Reynolds numbers are unreachable, so fine splash and turbulence detail is lower fidelity by construction.
open_questions: What sustained MLS-MPM throughput (particles x substeps per second) does a base iPhone 15 deliver under thermal throttling, in Metal compute and in Safari WebGPU? No published figure exists; this needs a week-one prototype.
Is scatter-style P2G with atomics or a gather-style formulation faster on Apple's GPU, and does either give run-to-run determinism for replays?

Does a PB-MPM-style solver converge acceptably in 3D with 4-8 iterations per frame? A later paper reports a predecessor failing to converge in 3D with few Jacobi iterations, and EA's 3D version is CPU-only and unpublished.
How stable and accurate is two-way coupling between an AVBD/XPBD rigid tier at frame rate and substepped MPM, particularly friction, stacking and stickiness at cm resolution?
What does an incompressible pressure solve cost on a 64^3-128^3 grid on the A16, compared with constraint-based or weakly compressible liquids?
Which modulus-softening rule is perceptually and physically acceptable, and at what wave-speed cap do players notice bounciness or compressibility?
Can a resolution-independent fracture criterion (fracture-energy regularized) work at dx = 2-5 cm without an extra phase-field solve?
Is a hashed sparse grid worth it on Metal/WebGPU at this scale, or does a dense moving 64^3-128^3 window win?

Unretrieved numbers that would sharpen the scaling estimate: Fei 2021 single-GPU per-substep timings, Young's modulus and dt; Flex Table 1; XPBI and CD-MPM timings. arxiv.org and www.math.ucla.edu need to be allowed for direct reads.
Can Warp or Taichi AOT target iOS in late 2026? Warp being CUDA/CPU-only and Taichi's maintenance status are from memory and unverified this session.

research:hardware.area: Real compute budget of a base iPhone 15 (A16 Bionic, 6 GB, 60 Hz) for a real-time first-principles physics engine
research:hardware.summary:
The base iPhone 15 is a 2 P-core + 4 E-core NEON-only CPU with a 5-core Apple8-family GPU (Metal 3 and Metal 4, fp32 only, float atomics yes, 64-bit atomics no), 6 GB LPDDR5 and a 60 Hz panel. Thermals, not peak speed or memory, set the budget: published stress tests put sustained GPU output at 50-85% of peak, and an A16 phone held about 4.3 W over a 30-minute game run.

Defensible per-frame budget at 60 Hz (16.67 ms), measured on a cool device (my derivation, not a published figure):
- GPU: at most ~10 ms total per frame, split as ~4-5 ms physics compute and ~5-6 ms rendering, so the frame still fits when the GPU throttles to ~60%.
- CPU: at most ~4 ms wall for physics on the 2 P-cores (about 6 P-core-ms), with the main thread under ~8 ms.
- Power: about 4 W average device draw, with thermalState staying at or below "fair" over a 20-30 minute soak.
- Fallback: 30 Hz rendering or half-speed simulation when thermalState reaches "serious".

What that buys, as estimates:
- MLS-MPM particles: roughly 10-17k sustained and 15-28k cool, with a quality screen-space fluid renderer. This is scaled from a native Metal app measured on an iPhone 18 Pro Max, and that app's tiers are ones that hold, not maxima. The optimistic ceiling is 50-100k with cheap rendering and 1-2 substeps, scaled from a WebGPU demo on a laptop iGPU.
- 2D rigid bodies: 5,050 stacked bodies cost 0.7-1.4 ms per step and 22,000 cost 2.8-4.9 ms on 1-2 M2 P-cores, which match A16 P-cores in single-thread speed.
- 3D rigid bodies: roughly 1,500-3,000 active stacked bodies in 4 ms. This is a rough estimate from a benchmark on unstated hardware.

Verification caveat: only developer.apple.com and raw.githubusercontent.com could be opened from this session. Findings marked verified=true come from those (Apple Metal tables dated 2026-10-23, the MSL 4.1 spec, Apple docs, forum threads and WWDC pages, LLVM, and project READMEs and benchmark CSVs). Everything from Wikipedia, UL, Notebookcheck, GSMArena, Geekbench and Codrops was seen only as search-engine excerpts and is marked verified=false; those hosts would need to be allowed in the session's network settings to open them directly. No published measurement of MPM, PBF or XPBD throughput on A15-A17 hardware was found.

findings.claim: A16 Bionic is GPU family Apple8 and supports both the Metal 3 and Metal 4 programming models; Metal 4 is available from Apple7 (A14) up. Apple8 has mesh shading, ray tracing, sparse textures, placement sparse buffers and textures (Metal 4), MetalFX temporal upscaling and floating-point atomics, but not 64-bit atomics on iOS (Apple9, A17 Pro and later).

Apple8 GPU limits: 1024 threads per threadgroup (theoretical; check maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup at runtime), 32 KB threadgroup memory, 31 buffer bindings per kernel, 16,384 px max 2D texture, 2,048 px max 3D texture per axis, 256M px texture-buffer width. MTLDevice.maxBufferLength is runtime-only; Apple documents only a 256 MB floor.

There is no fp64 on the GPU: the MSL 4.1 spec (2026-06-04) says Metal does not support the double type. atomic<float> works in device memory from Metal 3 (so on A16), and atomic float add/sub in threadgroup memory arrives only in Metal 4.1; 64-bit integer math is available from Apple3.

A16 CPU SIMD is 128-bit NEON only. LLVM's apple-a16 definition is ARMv8.6-A with NEON, FullFP16, FP16FML, DotProd, I8MM and BF16, and no SVE or SME; SME/SME2 first appear in apple-m4, where LLVM notes SVE is not supported by the core.

A16 has 6 CPU cores: 2 performance (Everest, up to 3.46 GHz) and 4 efficiency (Sawtooth, up to 2.02 GHz). The iPhone 15 uses the 5-core GPU variant at about 1398 MHz; the 4-core variant is in the iPad 11.

Geekbench 6 on iPhone 15 is about 2,570-2,670 single-core and 6,100-6,500 multi-core, against about 2,560-2,600 and 9,580-9,790 for an M2 MacBook Air. An A16 P-core therefore roughly equals an M2 P-core, but the A16 has 2 of them instead of 4.

A16 5-core GPU throughput: about 1.7-1.8 TFLOPS FP32 theoretical (third-party databases), Geekbench 6 Metal about 23.6-24.2k (M1 is about 32-34k), and 3DMark Wild Life Extreme of 2,868 at 17 fps on UL or 3,084 on GSMArena.

Sustained GPU output on A16 is 50-85% of peak depending on the test. Notebookcheck's iPhone 15 review reports a 15.7-24.7% slowdown after 20 3DMark stress loops (about 84% on Wild Life Extreme); GSMArena cites iPhone 15 GPU stability of 51% in one review and 71% in another; the A16 iPhone 14 Pro Max ranged 13.4-20.1 fps (67%) on the Wild Life Extreme stress test.

Power: iPhone 15 idles at about 0.94 W at 150 nits, averages about 4.85 W in Geekbench 5.5 and peaks at 13.6 W; the A16 GPU in GFXBench Aztec averages 7 W (5.84-9.88 W). In a 30-minute Genshin Impact run an A16 phone averaged 56.5 fps at 4.32 W, which puts the sustainable whole-device envelope near 4-4.5 W.

Apple's own guidance (WWDC18 session 612) is to design for sustained performance: "stay at 30 frames per second if you cannot sustain 60 for ten minutes or more". It says to monitor ProcessInfo.thermalState (nominal, fair, serious, critical) and Low Power Mode, and to pace frames with present(afterMinimumDuration:) rather than sleeping.

Measured native Metal MLS-MPM on an iPhone: the PhoneFluid app on a cool iPhone 18 Pro Max holds about 21k particles at 120 Hz (2.6 mm cells), about 43k at 60 Hz (2.1 mm) and about 76k at 60 Hz (1.7 mm), including screen-space refraction, caustics and foam. Its README says hot phones fall back to 60 Hz and half-speed liquid, and settled liquid stops simulating and drops to 30 Hz.

Scaling PhoneFluid to A16: the A20 Pro scores 64,069 on Geekbench 6 Metal against about 24k for A16 (about 2.7x), and 8,059 on Wild Life Extreme against 2,868 (about 2.8x). That gives roughly 15-28k MLS-MPM particles at 60 Hz on a cool iPhone 15 and roughly 10-17k after a 0.6 thermal derate; the PhoneFluid tiers are ones that hold, not maxima.
findings.source: Derived from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paulrobello/phone-fluid/main/README.md plus https://benchmarks.ul.com/en/hardware/phone/Apple+iPhone+18+Pro+Max+review and https://www.notebookcheck.com/Apple-A20-Pro-im-iPhone-18-Pro-begeistert-in-fruehen-Benchmarks.1395575.0.html (search excerpts only)

findings.claim: PhoneFluid's default P2G is a per-substep counting sort plus gather. Its shader comment says this avoids float atomics, which are "heavily contended on tiled GPUs when neighbouring threads share nodes"; the atomic<float> scatter path is kept only as an A/B option.

WebGPU-Ocean reports real-time MLS-MPM at about 100,000 particles on integrated graphics and about 300,000 on decent GPUs, at 2 simulation steps per frame. The same project's SPH with GPU neighbour search topped out at 30,000 on integrated graphics, and its P2G uses fixed-point atomicAdd because WGSL atomics are 32-bit integers only.
findings.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/matsuoka-601/WebGPU-Ocean/main/README.md (iGPU identified as Ryzen 7 5825U by https://tympanus.net/codrops/2025/02/26/webgpu-fluid-simulations-high-performance-real-time-rendering/, search excerpt only)

findings.claim: The Splash demo reached 1 substep per frame by lowering the Tait exponent from 5 to 1 and raising stiffness, trading incompressibility for stability. Its 1.6M-particle branch is described as very close to the WebGPU buffer-size limit.

WebGPU is supported and enabled by default in Safari on iOS 26, and Geekbench uploads show iPhone 15 running iOS 26.1 and 26.3. Default WebGPU limits are 256 MiB maxBufferSize, 128 MiB maxStorageBufferBindingSize, 8 storage buffers per shader stage, 256 compute invocations per workgroup and 2,048 max 3D texture dimension.
findings.source: https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/wiki/Implementation-Status (raw wiki opened); https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/main/spec/index.bs; iOS 26 on iPhone 15 from browser.geekbench.com search excerpt

findings.claim: Safari-specific limits for a PWA route: requestAnimationFrame is intentionally throttled to 30 fps in Low Power Mode, and a forum report shows a WebContent process killed at a 2,048 MB hard limit on a 12 GB iPhone 17 Pro.
findings.source: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=215745; Apple Developer Forums WebContent report (search excerpts only, exact thread not opened)

findings.claim: Apple does not publish per-app memory limits; os_proc_available_memory() is the supported way to read the remaining budget, and the increased-memory-limit entitlement is "only available on some device models". Forum measurements show a 2,098 MB hard limit on 4 GB iPhone 12 models and about 6,144 MB on 8 GB and 12 GB Pro iPhones with the entitlement.

For 6 GB iPhones the per-app limit is not established: unsourced blog tables give about 2.8 GB for an iPhone 14 and about 3.2-3.4 GB for 6 GB iPhones generally. No measurement for the base iPhone 15 was found.

Memory is 6 GB LPDDR5, listed as LPDDR5-6400 with a calculated 51.2 GB/s theoretical bandwidth by a third-party database. Apple claimed 50% more memory bandwidth than A15; no measured GB/s figure was found.

The base iPhone 15 display is a 6.1-inch 2556x1179 OLED at 60 Hz, so the frame period is 16.67 ms. The battery is 3,349 mAh / 12.98 Wh per a regulatory listing, so a 4.3 W load drains about 11% in 20 minutes.

Box2D v3 on an M2 Air with NEON, at dt 1/60 with 4 substeps: a 5,050-body pyramid costs 1.36 ms per step on 1 thread, 0.73 ms on 2 and 0.45 ms on 4. 22,000 bodies in 400 small pyramids cost 4.92 ms, 2.75 ms and 1.90 ms respectively.
findings.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erincatto/box2d/main/benchmark/m2air_neon/large_pyramid.csv and many_pyramids.csv; step and body counts from benchmark/main.c and shared/benchmarks.c in the same repo

findings.claim: The same Box2D scenes in the repo's 'm2air_float' build, which I take to be the non-SIMD build, cost 4.64 ms per step (5,050 bodies) and 17.8 ms (22,000 bodies) on 1 thread. That is a 3.4-3.6x penalty for not using NEON.

3D rigid-body data on mobile ARM is thin. A Godot-Rapier benchmark on unstated hardware lists a 10k-body 3D pyramid at 20.6 ms for Rapier3D and 25.1 ms for Jolt; a secondary blog cites about 925 steps per second for Jolt against 570 for PhysX and 220 for Bullet on Jolt's 3,680-body ragdoll scene. No Jolt, PhysX or Rapier numbers on A-series chips were found.
findings.source: https://godot.rapier.rs/docs/documentation/performance; https://jrouwe.nl/jolt/JoltPhysicsMulticoreScaling.pdf (not opened; numbers via secondary blog in search excerpt)

findings.claim: Vendor and engine guidance is coarse: Zibra estimates "tens of thousands of particles on mobile devices" in real time for its GPU MPM liquids, against hundreds of thousands on laptops. Unity's mobile guidance is to raise the fixed timestep from the 0.02 s default to 0.03-0.035 s for 30 fps targets, and an NVIDIA 2012 paper cites about 5 ms per frame as a typical game physics budget.

Thermal literature agrees that skin temperature, not junction temperature, is the binding limit in phones. A 2013 study put steady-state cooling near 1 W, with about 4 W sustainable for 240 s and 6 W for 100 s; a later Pixel 2 study notes SoC power can exceed 7 W, above the sustainable envelope.

Derived budget at 60 Hz, measured on a cool device: all GPU work within about 10 ms per frame (physics compute 4-5 ms, rendering 5-6 ms), CPU physics within about 4 ms wall on the 2 P-cores, and about 4 W average device power. The fallback is 30 Hz rendering or half-speed simulation at thermalState 'serious'.
findings.source: Derived from the thermal, power and Apple-guidance findings above (16.67 ms x 0.6 sustained fraction; 4.3 W 30-minute A16 game run)

implications: Thermals are the binding constraint, not peak speed or memory. Size every workload to about 60% of what a cool device can do, and build a thermal governor into the engine core that reads ProcessInfo.thermalState and measured GPU time.

The governor should change resolution, particle count or render rate, never the physical laws: keep a fixed physics timestep decoupled from rendering so behaviour stays deterministic when quality scales.

The invariant to budget is particle-substeps per frame. With roughly 4-5 ms of GPU compute, expect on the order of 10-30k MLS-MPM particles sustained with a good renderer, and that number falls linearly with substep count.

Explicit integration of truly stiff materials is out of reach. Steel's sound speed of about 5 km/s at 1 cm resolution needs microsecond timesteps, thousands per frame, so 'first principles' has to mean a multi-model design: rigid or constraint-based solids for stiff matter, MPM or similar for fluids, granular and soft matter, with implicit or position-based solvers where needed.
All GPU state must be fp32, since Metal has no double. Large worlds and SI units need local origins or scaled units, with any fp64 work kept on the CPU.
For particle-to-grid transfer on this tile-based GPU, plan on sort-plus-gather as the primary path and float-atomic scatter as a fallback. 64-bit atomics are unavailable on A16.
CPU design should assume 2 heavy threads at most, with the 4 E-cores for background and low-priority jobs. Write SIMD as 4-wide float NEON; skipping SIMD costs about 3.5x in the Box2D data.

A CPU rigid-body solver is affordable: a few thousand active 2D bodies cost about 1 ms on a P-core. 3D is likely limited to low thousands of active stacked bodies in 4 ms, so sleeping and islanding are mandatory.
Settled matter must stop simulating. The one measured iPhone MPM app sleeps resting liquid and drops to 30 Hz, and this is as much a thermal feature as a performance one.

Memory is not the limiting factor at these scales: 100k particles at 64-96 bytes is under 10 MB and a 128-cubed grid at 16 bytes per cell is about 34 MB. Keep the total footprint under about 2 GB, which is safe under every measured iPhone limit, and read os_proc_available_memory at launch.

Delivery path matters for the budget. With no Mac attached, WebGPU in Safari on iOS 26 is the route that works from a Linux container and fits the existing PWA repo, but it brings 256 MiB buffers, 128 MiB storage bindings, 8 storage buffers per stage, integer-only atomics, a roughly 2 GB web-process limit and 30 fps in Low Power Mode.

A native Metal build removes those limits and gives float atomics, 1024-thread groups and Metal 4, but needs a macOS build and signing step (for example cloud macOS CI). An engine core that targets both WebGPU and Metal keeps that option open.
Metal 4 is usable on A16, so the engine may adopt it, but nothing found suggests it raises compute throughput; treat it as optional.
open_questions: What is the actual jetsam limit for a foreground app on a base iPhone 15 under current iOS 26.x, with and without the increased-memory-limit entitlement, and does that entitlement apply to this model at all?
What do MTLDevice.maxBufferLength and recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize return on an iPhone 15?

What is the real A16 MLS-MPM throughput in particle-substeps per millisecond, for sort-plus-gather versus float-atomic scatter, and at what grid resolution? The 10-100k range here comes from scaling other hardware.
How much slower is WebGPU compute in Safari on iOS 26 than native Metal for the same kernels, and what are Safari's actual adapter limits on iPhone 15 (they may exceed the spec defaults)?

What steady-state throughput does the engine's own combined CPU+GPU duty cycle reach after 20-30 minutes at typical brightness, in and out of a case? Published stability figures range from 51% to 84% and none match this workload.
How fast is a Sawtooth E-core relative to an Everest P-core for physics jobs, and does iOS scheduling let a physics job system use the E-cores predictably? No independent per-core data was found.
What do Jolt, Box3D, Rapier or PhysX achieve on 2 A16 P-cores for 3D stacks and ragdolls? No measurements on A-series or comparable mobile ARM were found.

What do XPBD soft bodies or cloth and PBF/SPH fluids achieve on an A15-A17 class GPU? No published numbers were found; the only data point is SPH at about 30% of MLS-MPM particle count on a laptop iGPU.
Do placement sparse buffers (Metal 4, supported on Apple8) give a practical win for sparse simulation grids on A16?

research:toolchain.area: Build and delivery path (Linux cloud container to base iPhone 15), language/GPU API choice, and floating-point determinism — state as of 2026-11-23
research:toolchain.summary:
Ranked recommendation.

1. First on-device demo, least friction: ship the engine as a static web app. Compile a portable core to wasm32, run GPU kernels as WGSL compute through Safari's WebGPU, and serve it from GitHub Pages; the user opens the URL on the iPhone 15 and adds it to the Home Screen. This needs no Mac, no Apple account and no signing, and the whole loop runs from the Linux container with a git push. WebGPU is default-on from Safari 26 (iOS 26), which the iPhone 15 runs. Start single-threaded WASM SIMD plus GPU compute; add threads later through a COOP/COEP service-worker shim.

2. Path that does not cap long-term performance: the same core built as a native iOS app (Rust + wgpu on Metal, with room for hand-written Metal 3/4 kernels), built and signed on GitHub Actions macOS runners and delivered through TestFlight. This works without owning a Mac but needs the paid Apple Developer Program (US$99/yr). It removes the browser's roughly 2 GB process kill limit, the 4-thread cap, the missing haptics and the WebKit shader-compiler quirks.

3. Swift + Metal only: highest ceiling, but it cannot be compiled or tested in the Linux container and gives no web demo, so it is a later optimisation layer, not the foundation.

4. Free 7-day provisioning: needs hands-on Xcode on a Mac and weekly re-signing; not viable here.

Language/API: Rust + wgpu + WGSL is the only surveyed stack where one codebase and one shader language target both Safari WebGPU and native Metal with first-class support (wgpu v30.0.2, 12 Nov 2026). C++ with Emscripten/emdawnwebgpu has stable WASM threads but a weaker native-iOS story; Slang's Metal and WGSL targets are still marked experimental.

Determinism: CPU float determinism across ARM64, x86-64 and WASM is achievable and is what shipped engines do (no FMA contraction, no fast-math, own trig, fixed ordering; Jolt reports about 8% cost). GPU float results cannot be bit-exact across devices under the WGSL spec, so authoritative state must be CPU-side or integer on GPU.

Research limits: the shared web-search budget ran out late in the session, and only GitHub-hosted sources could be opened directly. webkit.org and caniuse.com have to be allowed in the session's network settings for direct checks, and developer.apple.com was not attempted after those failed, so Apple-documentation claims rest on search-result excerpts and are marked verified=false. No public Safari-WebGPU-versus-native-Metal compute benchmark was found, and the iPhone 15's actual adapter limits were not measured.

findings.claim: WebGPU is supported and enabled by default in Safari 26 on iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26 and visionOS 26; browser-compat-data lists navigator.gpu, GPUAdapter, compute pipelines, createQuerySet and the OffscreenCanvas 'webgpu' context as Safari/Safari-iOS 26, with nothing earlier.
iOS 26 and iOS 27 both support iPhone 11 and later, so a base iPhone 15 (A16) can run Safari 26/27 with WebGPU.

WebKit's Metal backend source hard-codes these compute limits for Apple6/Apple7-and-later GPUs: maxComputeInvocationsPerWorkgroup 1024, workgroup size 1024 per axis, maxComputeWorkgroupStorageSize 32 KB, maxComputeWorkgroupsPerDimension 65535, 44 storage buffers per stage, maxBindGroups 11, 2D textures 16384, 3D textures 2048.

On iOS WebKit computes maxBufferSize = max(256 MiB, min(1 GiB, MTLDevice.maxBufferLength / 3)) and sets maxStorageBufferBindingSize and maxUniformBufferBindingSize equal to it, so an iPhone exposes between 256 MiB and 1 GiB per buffer. A field report on an iPhone 14 Pro Max (A16, 6 GB, iOS 26.6.2 — same SoC and RAM as the iPhone 15) gives 1 GB for both.

WebKit always exposes shader-f16, indirect-first-instance, bgra8unorm-storage, dual-source-blending and clip-distances, adds ASTC/ETC2 on Apple GPUs, exposes timestamp-query when Metal stage-boundary counter sampling exists, and (on main) subgroups on Metal 3 devices. The A16 field report on iOS 26.6.2 saw shader-f16 but no subgroups, so shipped builds lag main.

WebKit's WGSL compiler is stricter than Chrome's Tint and wgpu's naga: it rejects constant arrays above 2,047 elements (Safari 27.3, reported 21 Nov 2026) and rejects binding a texture to a `let`, which broke every Bevy 0.20 PBR fragment shader in Safari 26.6 on macOS and iOS (issue opened 30 Oct 2026, still open).

iOS-only WebGPU stability reports exist: a Metal-backend crash that builds over about 70 seconds and scales with mesh count on iOS 26.0/26.1 (WebKit bug 302711), and a crash after about 500 WebGPU inferences on iOS 26.3 (onnxruntime #27584). On iOS, memory overuse typically kills the whole WebContent process and reloads the tab instead of firing device.lost.
findings.source: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=302711 ; https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/27584 (search excerpts, not opened) ; https://github.com/o2alexanderfedin/o2.services/issues/50 (opened, for the process-kill behaviour)

findings.claim: No rigorous public Safari-WebGPU-versus-native-Metal compute benchmark was found. The one measured data point is Chrome/Dawn on an M4 Max, where robustness bounds-check clamps cost about 14% of GPU time (63 ms vs 54 ms) in a storage-buffer-heavy shader.

In Safari (iOS mirrors desktop) WebAssembly threads/atomics and SharedArrayBuffer arrived in 15.2, fixed-width SIMD in 16.4 and GC in 18.2, but Memory64 and relaxed SIMD are listed only from Safari 27.3. Apple's 27.3 notes are a beta dated 3 Nov 2026 (search excerpt), so neither is in a shipping Safari yet.

SharedArrayBuffer needs cross-origin isolation, and GitHub Pages cannot set COOP/COEP headers. coi-serviceworker injects them from a service worker, reloads the page once on first load, and must be a separate same-origin file. Safari does not support COEP 'credentialless', so it must run in require-corp mode with all assets same-origin or CORP/CORS-enabled.

There is no documented fixed tab memory limit. A device log on an iPhone 17e (iOS 26.6.1) shows 'WebContent exceeded mem limit: ActiveHard 2048 MB (fatal)', and a WebAssembly.Memory declared with a 4 GB shared maximum was refused with 'RangeError: Out of memory'. Other reports put practical ceilings at about 1.5–3 GB on 6–8 GB iPhones, varying with uptime.

WebKit main gives iOS a 16 GB primitive address-space budget (64 GB elsewhere) and at most 3 signal-bounds-checked 'fast' WASM memories (8 elsewhere), so on iPhone the binding limit is the OS process memory kill, not address space.

WebKit's navigator.hardwareConcurrency returns 4 when the device has fewer than 8 cores and 8 otherwise, so a 6-core A16 reports 4. performance.now() resolution is 1 ms by default with a 20 µs high-precision mode (enabled for cross-origin-isolated pages, the trigger is from memory).

WebKit runs requestAnimationFrame at 60 fps and halves it to 30 fps for Low Power Mode, aggressive thermal mitigation, visually idle pages and cross-origin iframes the user has not interacted with; a page outside the viewport is throttled to one callback per 10 s.

Missing on iPhone Safari: navigator.vibrate, GamepadHapticActuator, ScreenOrientation.lock, pointer lock and navigator.deviceMemory; Element.requestFullscreen is 'Only available on iPad, not on iPhone'. A web build therefore has no haptics, and full-screen is only reachable as a Home Screen web app.

Available on iPhone Safari: DeviceMotionEvent/DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission(), Screen Wake Lock (working in Home Screen web apps since iOS 18.4), AudioWorklet (14.1), AudioContext.outputLatency (18.4), OPFS getDirectory and storage.persist (15.2), and OffscreenCanvas (16.4).

WebKit lets each origin store up to about 60% of disk in browser apps and Home Screen web apps (80% across all origins), but Safari deletes script-written data after seven days of browser use without user interaction unless persistence was granted.

Free 'Personal Team' provisioning needs Xcode and gives 7-day provisioning profiles, 10 App IDs and 3 devices; the paid Apple Developer Program is US$99/yr and includes TestFlight (builds valid 90 days, up to 100 internal testers with no Beta App Review) plus 25 Xcode Cloud hours/month. Xcode Cloud workflows are set up inside Xcode 15+, so it cannot bootstrap a no-Mac pipeline.

GitHub Actions 'macos-latest' is macOS 26 arm64 with Xcode 26.0.1–26.6 (default 26.6), iOS SDKs 26.0–26.5 and Rust 1.100 preinstalled; an Xcode 27 image (macOS 27.0.1) is in public preview. Standard macOS runners are free for public repositories and US$0.062/min for private ones, where the Free plan's US$12/month covers roughly 190 minutes.

fastlane with an App Store Connect API key supports certificate creation (cert), provisioning profiles (sigh), match and TestFlight upload (pilot) with 'No 2FA needed', so a CI macOS runner can build, sign and deliver with no Mac owned. Provisioning endpoints require a Team API key, not an Individual key, so the paid program is required.

Metal 4 (WWDC25, iOS 26) is supported on A14 Bionic and later, so the A16 qualifies. It adds explicit command queues/allocators, argument tables, residency sets (up to 32 per command buffer), a unified MTL4ComputeCommandEncoder (dispatches, copies, acceleration-structure builds), MTLTensor and a machine-learning encoder, and faster shader compilation — lower CPU overhead and explicit control, not new compute-shader capability.

wgpu's latest release is v30.0.2 (12 Nov 2026; v30.0.0 on 1 Jul 2026). Its README marks Metal on macOS/iOS and WebGPU on wasm as first-class, with WebGL2 best-effort; WGSL is passed straight to the browser on web and translated by naga to the native shading language elsewhere. MSRV is Rust 1.87.

wgpu's native Metal backend reports max_buffer_size as the full MTLDevice.maxBufferLength, without WebKit's divide-by-3 and 1 GiB cap, so the native path can bind larger buffers than Safari on the same phone.

Rust's aarch64-apple-ios and wasm32-unknown-unknown are both Tier 2 targets, but Rust threads on wasm still require a nightly toolchain with -Z build-std and +atomics,+bulk-memory (wasm-bindgen-rayon pins nightly-2025-11-15). Emscripten C/C++ reaches WebGPU through the external emdawnwebgpu port.

Slang's README still lists its Metal target as 'experimental' and its WGSL target as 'experimental — WGSL support is still work in-progress', so naga (WGSL to MSL) is the production cross-compilation path today.

Shipped engines: Bevy is Rust + wgpu (its WebGPU web build is still labelled 'experimental', WebGL2 is the web default, iOS goes through an Xcode project); Godot uses its own RenderingDevice over Vulkan/D3D12/Metal and supports the web only through its OpenGL Compatibility renderer. Leading game physics engines (Jolt in C++, Box3D in C17 with SSE2/AVX2/NEON, Rapier in Rust) are CPU-SIMD and multithreaded, not GPU.

Jolt achieves cross-platform determinism with a CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC build option that is 'approximately 8% slower', tested across MSVC, clang, gcc and emscripten and x86, ARM and RISC-V. Rapier's 'enhanced-determinism' feature cannot be combined with its simd or parallel features, and its WASM build is bit-identical across browsers, OSes and CPUs.

Box2D v3 reached cross-platform determinism (x64 and ARM; MSVC, GCC, Clang) by disabling FMA contraction (-ffp-contract=off), avoiding fast-math and replacing sinf/cosf/atan2f with its own implementations, with no noticeable performance cost reported.

WebAssembly's only floating-point nondeterminism is NaN bit patterns and sign; the other listed sources are shared-memory thread races, relaxed-SIMD instructions and resource exhaustion. Ordinary and fixed-width-SIMD float arithmetic in WASM is therefore bit-identical across engines and CPUs.

The WGSL spec specifies no rounding mode ('may round an intermediate result up or down'), allows 2.5 ULP error on division and 2 ULP on inverseSqrt (sqrt inherits it), lets fma() expand to an unfused multiply-add, permits flushing subnormals to zero, and makes NaN/Inf results indeterminate. Bit-exact float results across GPUs, drivers or browsers are not guaranteed.

implications: Structure the engine as a platform-agnostic core library plus thin hosts: a web host (wasm32 + browser WebGPU) for the first demo and a native iOS host (Metal via wgpu) for the long-term path. Rust + wgpu + WGSL gives both from one codebase; anything host-specific (haptics, audio, threads, storage) goes behind a platform interface.

Make the first deliverable a one-page capability probe on GitHub Pages that prints adapter.limits, features, crossOriginIsolated, hardwareConcurrency and a memory-growth test on the user's actual iPhone 15. Every budget below is inferred from other A16 devices or WebKit source, not measured on that phone.

Size GPU data structures for the web floor: any single buffer or binding at most 256 MiB guaranteed (1 GiB likely on A16), workgroups of at most 1024 invocations with 32 KB shared storage. Always request requiredLimits explicitly from adapter.limits; otherwise the spec defaults (128 MiB storage binding) apply.

Budget the web build at roughly 1 GB total process memory (WASM heap plus GPU buffers share the 6 GB unified RAM and the process is killed near 2 GB). Declare a modest WebAssembly.Memory maximum, never 4 GB, and do not plan on Memory64 or relaxed SIMD until Safari 27.3 ships.

Treat a tab kill as the normal failure mode, not device.lost: checkpoint world state to OPFS/IndexedDB, call navigator.storage.persist(), and make resume-from-snapshot a core engine feature (it is also what deterministic replay needs).
Run physics on a fixed timestep decoupled from rendering and make 30 fps presentation a supported mode, because Low Power Mode and thermal mitigation halve requestAnimationFrame on iOS.

Plan the web thread pool for at most 4 workers and gate it on crossOriginIsolated with a single-thread fallback. Starting single-threaded avoids both the coi-serviceworker reload dance and the Rust-nightly requirement for wasm threads; cross-origin isolation later also buys 20 µs timers for profiling.

Write WGSL to WebKit's stricter dialect from day one (no textures or samplers in let bindings, constant arrays of 2,047 elements or fewer, large tables in buffers) and test shaders on real Safari early; passing naga or Chrome validation does not mean Safari will compile them.

Split state by determinism class: rigid-body, constraint and gameplay-authoritative state on the CPU with strict IEEE rules (no FMA contraction, no fast-math, in-house sin/cos/atan2, fixed iteration and insertion order), and bulk continuum work (particles, grids, fields) on the GPU with tolerance-based, non-bit-exact guarantees or integer/fixed-point where exactness matters.

Use the WASM build as the cross-platform determinism reference: its float semantics are fixed by spec, so native ARM64 and x86-64 builds can be regression-tested against WASM state hashes in the Linux container.

For the native track, budget for the Apple Developer Program (US$99/yr) and a public repo (free macOS runners) or about US$0.062 per macOS minute; the pipeline is git push, macOS runner build and sign with an App Store Connect Team API key, TestFlight, install on the phone, with a fresh build at least every 90 days.

Keep an escape hatch below wgpu on native (raw Metal 3/4 kernels, larger buffers, Core Haptics, low-latency audio, all 6 cores with NEON). Metal 4 is optional on A16 and mainly reduces CPU-side overhead, so it is an optimisation, not a requirement.
Design game feel without haptics for the web build (navigator.vibrate and gamepad haptics are absent on iPhone) and expose haptics only through the native host.
Avoid Slang as the shader source of truth for now (Metal and WGSL targets experimental) and avoid a Swift-only or Metal-only core, which cannot be built or tested in the Linux container.
open_questions: What does the user's own iPhone 15 report for adapter.limits (maxBufferSize, maxStorageBufferBindingSize), features (timestamp-query, subgroups, shader-f16) and iOS/Safari version? Needs the probe page; MTLDevice.maxBufferLength for A16 was not found in any source.

How large is the real performance gap on A16 between Safari WebGPU, wgpu-on-Metal and hand-written Metal for the engine's own kernels (for example particle-grid transfers, constraint solves, neighbour search)? No public benchmark exists; needs a three-way microbenchmark.
What is the actual memory kill threshold on a 6 GB iPhone 15 for a Safari tab, a Home Screen web app and a native app, and how does it vary with uptime?
How long can the A16 sustain full GPU plus CPU load before thermal mitigation drops Safari to 30 fps, and what steady-state compute budget does that leave per frame?

Does coi-serviceworker work reliably inside an iOS Home Screen web app (first-launch reload, offline start, updates), and how well do 4 WASM worker threads scale on the A16's 2 performance + 4 efficiency cores?
What is the real Web Audio output latency on an iPhone 15 (speaker and Bluetooth), and is it low enough for physically driven sound? No measurements were found.

Can WGSL compute tests run headless in the GPU-less Linux container (software Vulkan through wgpu), and can WebKit's WGSL compiler be run in CI to catch Safari-only shader rejections before they reach the phone?

Will the user pay US$99/yr for the Apple Developer Program? Without it the native track has no practical no-Mac route; xtool (open-source Linux/Windows signing and install tool, 2.0 in beta) and similar sideloading tools exist but need a USB-connected computer and their requirements were not confirmed.
When does Safari 27.3 (Memory64, relaxed SIMD) reach general release, and is the user on iOS 26 or 27?
Is WebGPU usable inside WKWebView on iOS 26/27 for a hybrid shell? Compat data mirrors Safari 26, but Apple forum threads reported no GPU access; not resolved.
Does wgpu on iOS allow disabling naga bounds checks or other validation safely, and how much of the web-versus-native gap is validation versus API overhead?

Apple-side facts (provisioning limits, TestFlight terms, Metal 4 feature list, Xcode Cloud setup) were confirmed only through search excerpts because developer.apple.com, webkit.org and caniuse.com were not reachable from this environment; re-check them directly once those hosts are allowed.

research:contact.area: Rigid bodies, articulated mechanisms, contact and friction (solver families, sim-to-real trust, mobile ARM performance, determinism, physical sub-models, actuators, formats, coupling)
research:contact.summary: Recommendation: for mechanisms on an iPhone 15, the best realism per millisecond is a CPU, substepped soft-constraint Gauss-Seidel solver (the TGS-soft / "Soft Step" lineage of Box2D v3, Box3D and Rapier: semi-implicit substeps, warm starting, soft constraints, relax pass, graph-coloured NEON SIMD), extended with reduced-coordinate (Featherstone) articulations and physical actuator models for robots. That combination is what robotics stacks rely on (PhysX TGS + articulations, MuJoCo, Newton). It is the only family with published Apple-silicon throughput (Box3D on an M2: about 555 stacked boxes, 170 piled convex hulls or 900 jointed bodies per ms per core at 4 substeps), default cross-platform bitwise determinism, and proven stacking. XPBD-rigid has the cleanest physical compliance, but its authors and Erin Catto report stack, friction and float-precision problems. AVBD is promising for a GPU-unified rigid+soft solver but is experimental, with no mobile numbers. IPC/ABD give guarantees at roughly 35x to over 10,000x beyond the real-time budget on desktop CPUs. MuJoCo/Drake-style convex soft contact is the fidelity reference for articulated robots, not for thousands of free bodies. No engine is first-principles at the contact: all regularise stiffness by 4-6 orders of magnitude and treat Coulomb friction and restitution as empirical sub-models, and fitted simulators still miss real cube tosses by 13-25% of object size. The engine should therefore derive parameters from SI material data, clamp to what the substep rate resolves, and report the clamp. Couple to the deformable/fluid substrate in two tiers: constraint-level coupling inside the same substep loop for attached deformables, and partitioned momentum exchange (collider SDF/velocity out, accumulated wrenches in, asynchronous rates allowed) for bulk MPM/particle media on the GPU. Verification caveat: only GitHub-hosted sources could be fetched directly this session (box2d.org, arxiv.org, graphics.cs.utah.edu, newton-physics.github.io and matthias-research.github.io were blocked by the network allowlist, and the shared web-search budget ran out). Claims from sources I could not open are marked verified=false; URDF/SDFormat limits, hydraulic actuator models and the AVBD paper's tables remain unchecked.

findings.claim: Box3D v0.1 (Soft Step solver, 60 Hz, 4 substeps) on an Apple M2 Air with NEON: 5,050-box pyramid = 9.1 ms/step on 1 thread, 4.9 ms on 2, 2.8 ms on 4; 5,120-convex-hull pile = 30.1 / 15.8 / 8.6 ms; 9,900 bodies with 19,800 spherical joints = 11.0 / 5.8 / 3.1 ms. That is about 555 stacked boxes, 170 piled hulls or 900 jointed bodies per millisecond per M2 performance core (my division of published totals by timed steps).

Aggregator Geekbench 6 figures put the A16 at about 2,570-2,630 single-core versus about 2,600-2,620 for the M2, but only about 6,100 multi-core (5-core A16 variant) versus about 10,000 for the M2. M2 single-thread physics numbers should therefore transfer roughly 1:1 to one A16 performance core, of which the iPhone 15 has two.
findings.source: https://www.cpu-monkey.com/en/compare_cpu-apple_a16_bionic-vs-apple_m2 and nanoreview.net (search excerpts only; pages not opened)

findings.claim: Box2D v3 (2D, same solver family, 4 substeps) on M2 Air NEON: 5,050-body pyramid 1.36 ms/step single-threaded and 0.45 ms on 4 threads; about 10,000 bodies with 19,800 revolute joints 3.28 ms and 1.04 ms. Hand-written NEON made the contact solver 1.56x faster than scalar on the M2 (1,058 vs 679 fps), using 8 graph colours for 14,950 contact pairs.

XPBD (2016) ties constraint compliance to an elastic potential so stiffness is independent of time step and iteration count and yields constraint-force estimates. Small Steps (2019) showed n substeps x 1 iteration beats 1 step x n iterations: for a 1:1000 mass-ratio rigid chain, 100 iterations took 4 ms and visibly separated, 500 iterations took 17 ms and still stretched, 100 substeps x 1 iteration took 6 ms and was stiff; stated limits are that velocity error shrinks only linearly with dt and the dt^2 term can exhaust float32.

"Detailed Rigid Body Simulation with XPBD" (Mueller et al. 2020) uses 20 substeps x 1 iteration per 1/60 s frame (40 for pendula): 0.4 ms/frame for a robot arm, 3.5 ms for a rope, 18 ms for an RC car with soft tyres on a 3.6 GHz Core i7, and it drives a steering linkage with a 1:760 mass ratio. Its own stated drawbacks: reduced numerical damping leaves high-frequency jitter, small steps require double precision, and per-projection constraint updates "might cause instabilities when simulating tall stacks or piles of objects".

Erin Catto's Solver2D (Feb 2024) compared 8 solvers at 60 Hz (PGS, PGS_NGS, PGS_NGS_Block, PGS_Soft, TGS_Sticky, TGS_Soft, TGS_NGS, XPBD) and chose TGS_Soft (substepping + warm starting + soft constraints + relaxation, later renamed Soft Step) for Box2D v3, reporting trouble getting XPBD friction to work and floating artefacts from deriving velocity from positions. Box2D 3.0 notes say Soft Step is more stable than v2.4 for mass ratios, chains and stacks and over 2x faster, but slightly behind the old NGS block solver for vertical stacks.

Box3D (MIT, C17) was announced in late June 2026 and is at v0.1.0, which the author calls alpha: Soft Step solver, convex hulls / triangle meshes / height fields, graph colouring, wide SIMD (SSE2/AVX2/NEON), double-precision positions, recording/replay and cross-platform determinism. Joints are limited to revolute, prismatic, distance, motor, weld and wheel with an improved joint solver still planned, and the README lists only 64-bit Windows/Linux/macOS plus an Emscripten build (no iOS target named).

AVBD (Giles, Diaz, Yuksel; ACM TOG 44(4), Aug 2025) adds an augmented-Lagrangian dual update to Vertex Block Descent so hard contacts/joints and high stiffness ratios converge in a few implicit-Euler iterations; reported results are 110,000 blocks at 3.5 ms solve (9.8 ms with collision detection) and 510,000 blocks at 10.3 ms, with 4 iterations per frame on an RTX 4090. The paper notes hard constraints can inject energy through position correction (limited by a stabilisation parameter alpha) and that the hard-constraint Hessian needs an approximation to stay positive definite.

As of Nov 2026 every AVBD implementation I could open is explicitly non-production: the authors' 2D/3D demos are "not intended to be a super optimized implementation", Newton's SolverVBD (AVBD rigid) is marked experimental with limited joint support, three-avbd (WebGPU) lists no CCD, no sleeping and no cross-device bitwise determinism, and webphysics is a Chrome-only proof of concept. None publishes CPU or mobile-GPU timings.

MuJoCo uses generalized coordinates, where joint constraints "cannot be violated", and a convex soft-contact model that drops strict complementarity; defaults are a 2 ms timestep and solref 0.02 s / damping ratio 1, with the constraint time constant required to be at least 2x the timestep. Its docs concede that normal force and velocity can both be positive and "the only way to initiate slip is to generate some motion in the normal direction", and recommend elliptic cones, high impratio and the Newton solver (usually about 5 iterations, rarely over 20) to suppress slip.

MuJoCo is at 4.0.1 (11 Nov 2026); 2026 releases added a `discrete` integrator merging the constraint solve with the velocity update (3.13.0), an experimental penetration-free `ipc` flex-contact mode (3.14.0), sleeping-island work, and a `dcmotor` actuator with back-EMF, current saturation, cogging, inductance and thermal effects (3.12.0-4.0.0). Guidance: about 2 ms steps for contact-rich manipulation (0.5-2 ms for stiff grippers), 5-15 ms for locomotion, implicitfast by default, RK4 when long-horizon energy conservation of tumbling bodies matters.

MuJoCo C runs a single humanoid at about 650K steps/s on an Apple M3 Max using 2x numcore threads (1.8M on a 64-core AMD 3995WX). Assuming a 14-16-core chip that is on the order of 40K steps/s per core, about 25 microseconds per humanoid step, or roughly 0.2 ms per 60 Hz frame per robot at 500 Hz physics (my derivation).

Drake recommends hydroelastic over point contact unless simulation speed is a constraint, because point contact collapses a patch to one frame-inconsistent witness point and loses area effects such as torsional friction; hydroelastic moduli of 1e5-1e7 Pa already approximate rigid contact, versus about 2e11 Pa Young's modulus for steel. Hunt-Crossley dissipation is typically 20 s/m (over 500 s/m is unphysical), and Drake's convex discrete solvers resolve only dynamic friction, ignoring the static coefficient.

In the Acosta-Yang-Posa cube-toss validation (RA-L 2022), fitted simulators still missed real trajectories by 13.5 +/- 8.2% of cube width (Drake), 14.9 +/- 8.9% (Bullet) and 25.1 +/- 10.8% (MuJoCo) in position and 16.5-21.7 degrees in rotation, capturing inelastic impacts well but not elastic ones. Robot-learning stacks rely on reduced-coordinate articulations with TGS (PhysX default since 5.1; articulations have zero joint error by design) or on MuJoCo, and Hwangbo et al. (2019) closed ANYmal's sim-to-real gap mainly with a learned actuator model.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00541 ; https://nvidia-omniverse.github.io/PhysX/physx/5.4.1/docs/RigidBodyDynamics.html ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.10470 ; Hwangbo et al., Science Robotics 4(26) 2019 (all search excerpts only; hosts blocked)

findings.claim: Newton (Linux Foundation; Disney Research, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA; v1.8.0 in Nov 2026) is a Python/Warp, GPU-first engine (macOS is CPU-only) whose primary backend is MuJoCo Warp, alongside Featherstone and Steel (generalized coordinates), XPBD, VBD and Kamino (maximal coordinates), implicit MPM and Style3D cloth; only the MuJoCo solver supports equality constraints, and Kamino, VBD and Steel are marked experimental. Isaac Lab's solver guide maps workloads the same way: PhysX or MJWarp for articulated robots, Kamino for closed-loop mechanisms, VBD for cloth/soft/cables, MPM for fluids and granular media.

Reduced coordinates make tree joints exact but closed loops need added constraints; maximal coordinates treat loops and contacts uniformly but joints are enforced numerically, which MuJoCo's docs blame for "inaccuracies and instabilities when elaborate kinematic structures are involved" in game engines. Current engines hybridise: Rapier pairs impulse joints with reduced-coordinate multibodies (armature, per-DoF springs and DoF couplings added in 2026), and Disney's Kamino in Newton keeps maximal coordinates with a Proximal-ADMM solve aimed at kinematic loops with hard frictional contact.

Jolt uses a sequential-impulse solver with warm starting (documented as stable at 60 Hz with 1 collision step), supports iOS ARM64 with NEON, and offers cross-platform determinism via CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC at about 8% cost across x86, ARM, RISC-V and WASM. Its docs list limits: XPBD soft bodies collide only with rigid bodies, cylinders are the least stable shape, dynamic meshes are fairly expensive, LinearCast CCD ignores rotation and steals time, and double-precision positions cost 5-10%.

Rapier 0.36.1 (4 Oct 2026) has used a non-linear substep solver since 0.18 (Jan 2024) and removed legacy PGS in 0.29 (Sep 2025, up to 25% faster). 2026 releases added robotics-style multibody features (per-DoF armature and springs, DoF couplings, MJCF frictionloss as a constraint) and, in 0.36, soft bodies with plasticity/tearing plus an experimental FEM solver simulated together with rigid bodies, contacts and joints.

Cross-platform bitwise determinism exists today only in CPU solvers: Box2D v3 / Box3D by default across thread counts and x64/ARM with "no noticeable performance impact" (no fast-math, -ffp-contract=off, custom sin/cos/atan2; no rollback determinism), Jolt behind a flag at about 8% cost, Rapier via enhanced-determinism (combinable with multithreading since 0.35, not with 8-wide SIMD). MuJoCo's changelog only promises bit-identical results across thread counts for its batch API (3.17.0), and the WebGPU AVBD port states no cross-device bitwise determinism.
findings.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erincatto/erincatto.github.io/master/posts/2024/08/determinism/index.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erincatto/box3d/main/docs/simulation.md ; Jolt Architecture.md ; Rapier CHANGELOG.md ; MuJoCo changelog.rst ; https://github.com/sbobyn/three-avbd

findings.claim: IPC (Li et al. 2020) guarantees intersection- and inversion-free steps, but its own table reports 1.4-776 s of compute per time step (h = 0.01-0.04 s) for 3K-67K-node scenes on 4-8-core desktop CPUs, and 0.05 s per step even for a 216-node arch. That is roughly 35x to over 10,000x slower than real time on desktop hardware (my ratio of compute time to step size).

Affine Body Dynamics (Lan et al. 2022) reports 124x to over 1,200x speed-ups over rigid-IPC on CPU and per-frame times near Bullet's in one test (about 2.2 ms vs 1.5 ms at 1/240 s); its GPU successors are CUDA-bound (StiffGIPC: up to 10x over prior GPU IPC; libuipc). Offset Geometric Contact (2025) reaches 6.3 ms per step for a 246K-vertex cloth stack on an RTX 4090 (0.21 s on CPU), about two orders of magnitude faster than IPC, but only while per-step motion stays within the contact radius.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2201.10022v1 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06224 ; https://graphics.cs.utah.edu/research/projects/ogc/ (search excerpts only; hosts blocked)

findings.claim: Genesis (academic release Dec 2024; Apache-2.0; rigid, FEM, MPM, PBD/SPH, uipc and a SAP coupler in one Python scene, compiled to CUDA/Metal/Vulkan/x86/ARM64) advertised 43M FPS, which an independent analysis reduced to about 0.29M FPS (150x lower) under representative settings and measured as 3-10x slower than ManiSkill on cube picking. Its IPC coupling requires an NVIDIA GPU on Linux/Windows x86 per the README.

Engines bolt extra empirical terms onto Coulomb friction: MuJoCo's condim 4/6 add torsional and rolling friction whose coefficients have units of length (contact-patch radii; rolling default 0.0001), Box2D v3.1 caps rolling-resistance torque at coefficient x radius x normal force, and XPBD-rigid applies static friction positionally while lambda_t < mu_s * lambda_n with dynamic friction in a separate velocity pass. Drake's convex discrete solvers drop the static coefficient entirely.
findings.source: MuJoCo doc/modeling.rst ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erincatto/box2d/main/docs/simulation.md ; PBDBodies.pdf ; Drake contact_model_doxygen.h (all opened)

findings.claim: Restitution is approximated everywhere: Box2D/Box3D solve it after the main pass from pre-solve approach speed (approximate with multiple contacts, zeroed below a threshold), and XPBD-rigid sets e = 0 when |v_n| <= 2|g|h. Resolvable stiffness is tied to step rate in every engine read: Box2D/Box3D and Jolt cap soft-constraint frequency at half the step frequency, MuJoCo's default contact time constant is 20 ms (10x its 2 ms step), and Drake warns fixed-step penalty contact becomes unstable above about one tenth of the contact time scale.
findings.source: Box2D and Box3D docs/simulation.md ; PBDBodies.pdf ; Jolt Architecture.md ; MuJoCo doc/modeling.rst ; Drake contact_model_doxygen.h (all opened)

findings.claim: Coulomb friction is an empirical law that omits the Stribeck effect, drilling friction and viscous terms, and rigid bodies with Coulomb friction can have no solution or several (Painleve paradox), resolved only by impulsive forces or contact compliance. The coefficient of restitution is not a material constant: for viscoelastic bodies it tends to 1 as impact speed goes to 0, and in the plastic regime it falls roughly as v^(-1/4).
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03545 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0204105 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0701142 (search excerpts only; host blocked)

findings.claim: Box2D 3.0 replaced its CCD with a hybrid speculative + time-of-impact scheme that "seems to prevent almost all dynamic versus static tunneling"; dynamic-vs-dynamic CCD is off by default and opt-in bullets are less robust (same policy in Box3D). Jolt's LinearCast uses the starting orientation so fast-rotating long objects can still tunnel, and PhysX CCD is disabled when GPU dynamics is on.
findings.source: erincatto.github.io posts/2024/08/releasing-box2d-3.0 ; Box3D docs/simulation.md ; Jolt Architecture.md ; IsaacLab docs/source/concepts/solver_differences.rst (all opened via GitHub)

findings.claim: Shape choice dominates cost and stability: in Box3D's M2 data a pile of 5,120 convex hulls costs about 5.9 microseconds per body-step versus 1.8 for stacked boxes (3.3x, my division); Jolt calls dynamic meshes fairly expensive and cylinders its least stable shape; Drake's hydroelastic cost scales with the number of contact-surface faces. SDF contact for non-convex parts appears only as experimental or plugin paths in the sources opened (three-avbd's SDF playground is capped at 36 bodies; MuJoCo ships an SDF plugin).
findings.source: Box3D benchmark CSVs ; Jolt Architecture.md ; Drake contact_model_doxygen.h ; https://github.com/sbobyn/three-avbd ; MuJoCo changelog.rst

findings.claim: MuJoCo's actuator model separates transmission, activation dynamics and force generation, and its tuning guide states that geared actuators add reflected rotor inertia I_rotor * N^2 that "often exceeds the link inertia of wrists, fingers, and ankles", so realistic armature "improves realism, mass-matrix conditioning, and timestep stability for free". Viscous joint damping is integrated implicitly at no solver cost, whereas dry frictionloss adds a constraint row per joint.

MJCF is being ingested beyond MuJoCo (Rapier 0.35.3 handles MJCF frictionloss as a constraint; Newton ships a MuJoCo-to-USD converter), while MuJoCo's OpenUSD support is still labelled experimental and uses standard UsdPhysics plus mjcPhysics extensions, with Newton's USD schemas acting as staging for solver-agnostic additions (REP-158 discussion, June 2026). Only the Rapier changelog entry and MuJoCo's USD decoder plugin were opened directly; the rest is from search excerpts.
findings.source: https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/latest/OpenUSD/mjcPhysics.html ; https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco/discussions/3360 ; https://github.com/newton-physics/mujoco-usd-converter (search excerpts) ; Rapier CHANGELOG.md and MuJoCo changelog.rst (opened)

findings.claim: Published rigid-deformable coupling in the substep solver family is done at constraint level inside the substep loop: Small Steps notes that liquid and rigid constraint lists are "simply concatenated or interleaved, allowing fine-grained coupling", Mueller 2020 couples soft tyres to rigid rims this way, Rapier 0.36 simulates soft bodies together with rigid bodies, contacts and joints, and Newton's VBD handles cloth, soft and rigid bodies in one solver. Jolt's XPBD soft bodies collide with rigid bodies only (no soft-soft collision, no buoyancy), and Isaac Lab lists Newton's MPM with rigid bodies as colliders only.
findings.source: smallsteps.pdf ; PBDBodies.pdf ; Rapier CHANGELOG.md ; newton docs/solvers/index.rst ; Jolt Architecture.md ; IsaacLab solver_differences.rst (all opened)

implications: Core solver: build on a CPU, substepped soft-constraint Gauss-Seidel solver (TGS-soft / Soft Step lineage: semi-implicit Euler per substep, warm starting, soft constraints, relax pass, graph-coloured 4-wide NEON), 60 Hz frames with 4-8 substeps globally and 16-32 for flagged precision islands. Keep XPBD-rigid as a reference for position-level compliance, not as the primary contact solver.

Budget: the M2 data gives about 1,030 boxes/ms or 325 convex hulls/ms on two performance cores at 4 substeps. Plan the iPhone 15 rigid slice at 3-4 ms, i.e. roughly 3,000 awake boxes or 1,000 hulls, fewer at 8 substeps (solver cost scales with substeps, collision does not), before thermal derating and any WebAssembly overhead. Islands, sleeping and per-island substep counts are mandatory.

Mechanism path: add reduced-coordinate articulations (Featherstone ABA/CRBA) as first-class bodies inside the same substep loop, with exact joints, armature = N^2 * rotor inertia, implicit joint damping, and friction-loss rows only where stiction matters. Apply contacts and loop closures as soft constraints through the articulation's impulse response; keep maximal-coordinate joints for breakable, loosely constrained or loop-heavy assemblies.

Actuators belong to the physics layer: DC motor (voltage, back-EMF, winding resistance, current limit giving the linear torque-speed envelope), gearbox (ratio, reflected inertia, efficiency, backlash as a soft equality), springs/dampers and fluid-power cylinders as stateful models, following MuJoCo's transmission + activation + force-generation split. Robotics evidence says actuator fidelity dominates sim-to-real error.

Materials-first parameterisation: author density, Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, friction pairs and dissipation in SI, derive contact stiffness/damping (Hertz + Hunt-Crossley) and joint compliance from them, then clamp to what the substep rate resolves (soft-constraint frequency at most 1/2 to 1/4 of substep rate) and report the clamp. Steel-on-steel stiffness cannot be resolved at 480-960 Hz; effective contact moduli will be in the 1e5-1e7 Pa range that Drake also accepts.

Label friction and restitution as empirical sub-models: Coulomb cone with persistent anchors, optional static/kinetic and Stribeck curve, torsional and rolling resistance scaled by the computed contact-patch radius, restitution from contact dissipation with a resting-velocity threshold. Keep the normal direction compliant rather than perfectly rigid to avoid Painleve-type non-existence.

Energy policy: no hidden numerical damping in the rigid core (semi-implicit substeps, implicit gyroscopic term), all dissipation explicit and material-derived. Ship a conformance suite with energy/momentum drift budgets (triple pendulum, 1:1000 chain, heavy-on-light stack, Newton's cradle, spinning coin, card pyramid) plus a reality check against the published cube-toss data, where fitted Drake/Bullet/MuJoCo still sit at 13-25% position error.

Collision: analytic primitives and convex hulls first (hull piles cost about 3.3x boxes per body), convex decomposition for concave dynamic parts, triangle meshes and height fields static-only, SDF contact reserved for gears/threads after a prototype. Use hybrid speculative + time-of-impact CCD against statics with opt-in bullets, and run broad/narrow phase once per frame with speculative margins.

Determinism: keep the rigid/mechanism core on CPU in float32 with strict floating-point rules (no fast-math, FMA contraction off, own sin/cos/atan2, creation-order processing). Because development happens on x64 Linux without a Mac, x64-to-ARM64 bit-exactness is what lets CI golden trajectories stand in for on-device behaviour; treat the GPU substrate as non-deterministic and isolate it behind the coupling interface.

Coupling tier A (attached deformables: tyres, belts, cables, pads, cloth on mechanisms): solve them in the same substep loop as compliant particle/FEM constraints interleaved with the rigid sweep, sharing the SI material model, as Mueller 2020, Rapier 0.36 and Jolt do.

Coupling tier B (bulk continuum: MPM/SPH/PBF fluid, granular, large soft volumes, likely on GPU): partitioned momentum exchange. Rigid bodies export collider SDF + velocity, the substrate returns per-body wrenches accumulated over its own steps, applied as impulses at rigid substep boundaries, with asynchronous rates allowed and explicit momentum bookkeeping.

Do not base the phone runtime on IPC/ABD, Newton, Genesis or libuipc: IPC costs 1.4-776 s per step on desktop CPUs and the fast variants are CUDA/Python-bound. Use them as offline ground truth and for asset compatibility (MJCF import first, USD Physics second).
Treat AVBD as a time-boxed R&D track (Metal/WebGPU unified rigid + soft), not the baseline: no mobile numbers, implicit-Euler damping, experimental joints and no bitwise determinism as of Nov 2026.

Build-vs-adopt input: Box3D (MIT, C17, alpha v0.1, Soft Step, NEON, deterministic, Emscripten build, few joint types), Jolt (iOS ARM64 supported, deterministic including WASM, mature joints/vehicles, sequential impulse) and Rapier (Rust, multibodies + soft bodies + determinism) are viable bases or reference implementations. None provides material-derived contact or actuator physics, which is the layer this engine must add.
open_questions: Real iPhone 15 throughput: sustained (thermally throttled) bodies per ms for a Soft-Step-style solver on 2 performance + 4 efficiency cores, native versus WebAssembly (128-bit SIMD, threads). No published A16 or iPhone physics benchmark was found; the M2 figures are a proxy.

Substep count versus fidelity for mechanisms: how many substeps do gear trains, 1:1000 mass-ratio linkages and stiff springs need, and does float32 hold? Macklin and Mueller both warn about precision at small steps, and NEON doubles halve SIMD width.
